name: Smile practice / smile maxxing

lead: Smile maxxing means practicing and refining one's smile, usually in a mirror, to look warmer or more attractive.
Studies show smiles influence how likable people seem, and that genuine and posed smiles differ, but no trials test smile training as such.

paras: Practitioners aim to use the muscles around the eyes as well as the mouth. Facial feedback research suggests expressions may slightly affect mood.
No medical risks reported. Cultural context affects how smiles are read.

lead: Smile practice, or smile maxxing, is the practice of training one's smile, often in a mirror, to look more natural, symmetrical or attractive. Community discussion focuses on the difference between a polite and a genuine smile and on how smiling is perceived.

Research distinguishes the Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eyes, from the voluntary "Pan Am" smile using only the mouth muscle.[1] Studies report smiling can make people seem more likable and approachable, though perceptions differ across cultures.[1] The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that expressions also influence emotion; a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies found small but robust effects.[2]

paras: Guillaume Duchenne described two smile types in 1862. The Duchenne smile raises the mouth corners and the cheeks via the orbicularis oculi, and was reported by Messinger, Fogel and Dickson (2001) to be uniquely associated with positive emotion.[1] Botox use may weaken eye muscles and limit this smile.[1]

Gladstone (2002) found smiling makes people seem more likable and approachable, while Krys et al. (2016) found that in some cultures a smiling person may be seen as less intelligent.[1] Smiling is more common in the US and France than China or Japan.[1]

Strack, Martin and Stepper (1988) reported that holding a pen between the teeth made cartoons seem funnier. A 17-lab replication led by Wagenmakers (2016) found no systematic effect, a later study attributed the difference to a camera, and Coles, Larsen and Lench (2019) found small effects overall (d about 0.2).[2]
No studies found on smile practice or smile training as a looksmaxxing method. Related research on facial feedback and smile perception is described above.[1][2]

timeline.event: Duchenne describes two types of smile.[1]
Strack, Martin and Stepper pen study.[2]
Coles, Larsen and Lench meta-analysis of 138 studies.[2]
